title: An overview of gradient descent optimization algorithms
focus: Explain plain gradient descent and momentum (Sections 2 and 4.1) on a 1-D quadratic loss f(θ) = a·θ². The learner sets the learning rate η, the curvature a, the starting point and the momentum γ. Show the loss curve with the iterates on it and the loss over iterations. Guide them through a learning rate that converges smoothly and one that diverges. Check that with η·a below 1 plain gradient descent converges toward θ = 0 and that η·a above 1 makes it diverge.
excerpt:
2 Gradient descent variants

Gradient descent is a way to minimize an objective function J(θ) parameterized by a model's parameters θ ∈ R^d by updating the parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient of the objective function ∇θJ(θ) w.r.t. to the parameters. The learning rate η determines the size of the steps we take to reach a (local) minimum.

3 Challenges

Choosing a proper learning rate can be difficult. A learning rate that is too small leads to painfully slow convergence, while a learning rate that is too large can hinder convergence and cause the loss function to fluctuate around the minimum or even to diverge.

4.1 Momentum

SGD has trouble navigating ravines, i.e. areas where the surface curves much more steeply in one dimension than in another. Momentum is a method that helps accelerate SGD in the relevant direction and dampens oscillations. It does this by adding a fraction γ of the update vector of the past time step to the current update vector:

v_t = γ v_{t−1} + η ∇θJ(θ)
θ = θ − v_t

The momentum term γ is usually set to 0.9 or a similar value.
